review:
10/10 Mental Health Destroyer

I opened my first cases in CS:GO over a decade ago, and now here I am in CS2, still buying the same AWP skins and getting headshot through smokes I swear were totally covering me.

This game is a masterclass in psychological warfare. Within two minutes of loading into a Premier match, you will encounter a 12-year-old shouting orders like a veteran drill sergeant, a player who hasn't spoken a word all game suddenly dropped a sick 1v4 clutch, and at least two teammates passionately debating tactical setups in Russian.

The strategy is simple and timeless. If your team is winning, you push Mirage A site like tactical geniuses. If your team is losing, you type "RUSH B DON'T STOP MY BROTHERS" in team chat, buy a Mac-10 with no armor, and run blindly through a molotov while screaming down the microphone.

CS2 brought us shiny new graphics, realistic volumetric smokes that actually react to grenades, and sub-tick servers that make you question every shot you miss. But under all the fancy new engine polish, it is still the exact same chaotic masterpiece we all fell in love with.

You will get tilted, you will lose rounds you should have won, and you will threaten to uninstall it every single weekend. Then you will open Steam five minutes later, queue up for another match, and do it all over again.

Best game ever made.

review:
Unfair Punishment System Is Ruining Dota 2

I have spent a significant amount of time and money on Dota 2, but I am extremely disappointed with the current punishment system.

The game repeatedly gives me Low Priority penalties, ranked matchmaking restrictions, and reduces my Behavior Score and Communication Score, even when the situation involves temporary technical issues rather than intentional misconduct.

Sometimes my internet connection drops or my computer freezes. I always try to reconnect within a few minutes, but the system still treats me as if I deliberately abandoned the game.

In one of my recent matches, I was simply taking my time to choose a hero. I was still connected to the game, yet I received another penalty.

My Behavior Score and Communication Score have now dropped to critically low levels, making the overall matchmaking experience increasingly frustrating.

The worst part is that the system creates a vicious cycle: once your scores drop, recovering them becomes extremely difficult.

I regularly purchase in-game items and have financially supported this game because I genuinely enjoy Dota 2. However, spending money on a game that repeatedly punishes you without properly considering the circumstances feels incredibly disappointing.

Valve needs to seriously reconsider how its automated punishment system works. There should be a clear distinction between intentional griefing, abandoning games on purpose, and temporary technical difficulties.

Players deserve transparency, fairness, and the opportunity to appeal questionable penalties.

I cannot recommend Dota 2 in its current state.

Until Valve improves its punishment system and starts taking legitimate player complaints seriously, my review will remain negative.

review:
Having loved the original [i]Portal[/i], I felt immediately at home with its sequel. It retains the same trademark humor, clever plot twists, and wonderfully simple controls while building on everything that made the first game so enjoyable.

The real beauty of [i]Portal 2[/i] lies in its elegant simplicity. The puzzles are meticulously crafted, gradually introducing new mechanics and teaching you how they work before challenging you to combine them in increasingly creative ways. The learning curve feels natural, and every new mechanic opens up fresh possibilities without overwhelming you.

There were a few occasions when I had to stop and think, but I never felt truly stuck. Experimenting with different ideas, trying unexpected approaches, or simply looking at the room from a different perspective often led me toward a solution. There's something immensely satisfying about that moment when everything suddenly clicks into place.

One tip for anyone playing: [b]look at the exit and work backward.[/b] Figuring out where you need to go and what needs to happen to get there is often the key to solving a puzzle.

A brilliant sequel that builds on the original's strengths without losing any of its charm.

You could also speedrun to your heart's content, and challenge yourself in the pits of darkness slaying foes, gathering every item and resource, completing every milestone and achievement that there is to offer (if you dare to go for the last two achievements in this game...wishing you the best of luck). There are numerous opportunities with every new farm you start, so things don't feel too repetitive. It's not hard to find different ways to spice up your playstyle or goals and experiences for a new farm.

There are also options with playing the game vanilla, or adding mods to your experience. But nonetheless, if you enjoy cozier games that let you take your time, cultivate a farm and enrich the community around you; and can also challenge you in some unexpected ways, depending on your approach, you'll likely enjoy this game. 

Whenever things get tough and some distraction is needed from the real world to level your head, Stardew is usually the first place many people go to, including myself. Stardew Valley can give people a space of comfort in today's world. And the authentic creativity required to make this game is a joy to see, and respectable.
Also, the soundtrack is amazing, vibes are great. 10/10.

review:
TL;DR it's peak

I miiiiiiight have gotten slightly addicted to this game, but in my defense, it's tons of fun. The graphics are incredible, the music rocks, and the open world lets you go at your own pace. You can farm crops as well as raise animals (I recently got the Deluxe Barn and a sheep let's go); depending on how you play and what you want to accomplish, there isn't a "wrong" way to go about playing the game.

There are several advancements that keep you from getting bored. Without getting into spoilers, you can mine in the caves, develop friendships and romance, forage for wild plants, and even fish. (I am terrible at the fishing minigame, but maybe you won't be!) There's also the option to forage around in trashcans if you wish to do a bit of trolling.

There's a loose overarching story, but day-to-day life consists of working on your farm, mining, etc. It definitely lives up to its cozy reputation, but there are some deeper elements thrown in there such as an evil corporation and more somber elements in some characters' arcs. You're not being railroaded into liking a certain character or doing a certain thing on a certain day (other than celebrating festivals, but you technically don't HAVE to go to those). So yeah, I'd say this game is pretty lit.

review:
Somewhere between 350 and 480 hours depending on how Steam decides to count it. Either number is more than anything else in my library, and I have a lot of games in there that I love. I want to be clear about what that number is not. It is not because Stardew is the deepest game I own, or the hardest, or the one with the best story. It is because it is the one I can always come back to. Bad week, nothing else clicking, brain fried from work, I load the farm and I know exactly what I am doing for the next two hours and I know I am going to feel better at the end of it. There are maybe three games in my life that can do that reliably and this is the one that has done it the longest.

The thing people get wrong when they call it a cozy game is that it is actually a planning game wearing a cozy game as a coat. Every season is a deadline. Crops have a window and if you plant the wrong thing on the wrong day you eat the loss. The mines have a rhythm, the deeper floors want you to come prepared, and the first time you figure out which floors the iron actually lives on you feel like you unlocked something. The community center is a checklist that quietly organizes your entire first year without ever telling you it is doing that. And every single day, every day, you are making small tradeoffs about energy and daylight that add up. Do I water or do I fish. Do I go to the mines or do I talk to someone. Do I spend the money on seeds or do I save it for the building. None of those decisions are big. All of them matter. That is the exact part of my brain that Factorio and Timberborn and Banished scratch, it is just running at a slower heartbeat here, and that slower heartbeat is why I can play it when I cannot play anything else.

The farm is never finished. That is the hook and it never dulls. You can minmax it into a greenhouse money printer or you can wander around fishing for a season because you felt like it and the game is equally happy. I have done both. I have had farms I laid out like a spreadsheet and farms I let grow weird and ugly and loved more. It meets you wherever you are that week.

Then there is the question of who made it. One guy. One guy built this, scored it, drew it, wrote every villager, and has kept it alive for a decade without charging for it twice. The 1.6 update dropped years after launch and added a whole new layer to a game people already thought was done. Green rain, new events, new fish, new reasons to go back. He just handed it to everyone. I am not sentimental about developers but I think that matters, and I think you can feel it in the game. Nothing in Stardew is there because a meeting decided it should be. It is all there because one person thought it would be nice. That is a different texture than a game made by a hundred people and you notice it.

I will say one honest thing against it. The first spring is slow, on purpose, and if you come in expecting the game to tell you what it is about you will bounce. It does not explain itself. It just hands you a watering can and some parsnip seeds and lets you figure out that the real game starts once you have a little money and a little confidence and a reason to care about the people in town. Push through to summer. It opens up.

If you have never played it, play it. If you have played it, you already know everything I just said and you probably have your own version of the bad week story. That is kind of the point. Shout out to ConcernedApe.

review:
Holy crap, 4607 hours in this game and I still haven't dropped a review? 

This game is The Best Game In Existence. Hands down. Literally the only game that I have absolutely zero complaints about the game play itself, and absolutely love the story. 

The very few complaints I had earlier in the game's existence, have all been fixed in subsequent patches (thank you for making snake tail skeletons easier to find, omg that was giving me the irrates!!)

I only have one serious complaint, and it relates to ableism in the story. I have a big issue with the cut scene between Penny and George, and to a lesser extent between Harvey and George:

The player arrives to see George struggling to reach something, and then Penny walks in and just does it for him, without asking whether he wants help. For those of us in the disabled community, we know just how frustrating an experience this can be. You should ask us before getting involved! Maybe we would like some help, but it removes our power over our own lives when people don't even ask what we want. 

George's reaction to get angry about this is completely natural and understandable. However, if the player sides with George in the resulting dialogue, we lose friendship points with Penny and gain nothing with George. 

Penny being the sort of ernest and caring person she is, I feel would actually want to be educated about how things are for disabled people, and how important it is to respect our agency and autonomy. I wouldn't necessarily expect to gain friendships points with her for giving her the critical feedback, but I really don't think we should be penalised for taking the ethicial dialogue option. 

Similarly, when Harvey is giving George his doctor's recommendations, I chose the option to tell Harvey that the choice of how he lives his life is ultimately up to George - and lost friendship points with Harvey for it. 

I just skip both these scenes every time now. 

I deeply love and appreciate Eric Baroney and this masterpiece of a game he has created. But I would truly love it if he could learn a bit about issues facing disabled people, and help advocate for us in his dialogue options and resulting bonuses. At the very least, supporting George should earn us friendship points with him, surely??

review:
If we  ignore that they are using 5th edition rules, instead of Pathfinder or 3.5e... this is basically as good as a crpg can ever get at least story, replayability, production (visuals, music, sound, motion capture, yo name it) and emotional impact wise. 
It is a colossal achievement, especially if you consider that it is a relatively low level adventure (caps at 12) as opposed to semi godly stuff of BG2. Because of the 5th edition I wont give it a 100%, a few annoyances here and there I have to take some points out, so I will give it a 99.999%. 

The value you can get from this game as immersive entertainment is just extraordinary. They could be charging $500 and it would still be cheap and worth it as weird as this sounds. The replayability of it is a weird thing because even though you KNOW the story more or less and even if you played it once thoroughly, you have so many choices that ending up mattering one way or another, so you want to replay it just so that you see their impact playing out too. I cannot overstate this fact.

Two things you cannot really do. 
1) honor mode it without having played the hell out of it first. I mean you could but you wont beat it. It is like a real tabletop session. You will either do something stupid or you will get unlucky and you ll die. 
2) you cannot avoid the min maxing to a certain extend and unfortunately there are countless of guides on how to game the system that frankly will ruin your experience. This is a problem that all crpgs have though so I am not sure why I am bringing it up. 

In any case. This is it. As of 2026 the apogee of game development really for the CRPG (D&D style in particular) genre. There are others like e.g. Pathfinder which are also extremely good, but BG3 is incredibly special. 
I cannot remember another game including BG1 and BG2 where I cared in such a way about the characters. Or that it was so often morally grey. If you are old school D&D you may have some trouble with playing a Paladin properly, it is one of the reasons for the 99.999% (e.g. there are cases where if you play 100% as a paladin, you will simply die, so you will have to do something that normally would be impossible for a paladin, you 'd become an oathbreaker or worse) but given the magnitude of awesome that everything else in the game is, voice acting, motion, tactics, music, sound design, visuals, the whatever flaws that one can find can be completely ignored. 

This could have been released as 10+ different campaigns (e.g. like the temple of elemental evil) and yet it is a coherent highly repeatable colossal amalgamation of all of them. 

LTDR; This is one for the ages, and I suggest you buy it and PLAY it if you have the time because there are not many or any like it out there.

review:
Truly, inarguably, one of the greatest games of our generation, if not of all time.

I was intimidated at first by the sheer scale and intricate depth of this game, and I played the first two hours assuming I would end up going for a refund. That was the wrong approach, it turns out, and I very quickly burned out. When I came back months later, ready to give this thing a real chance and unafraid to dive in, the magnetism was instant. I have one completed playthrough and a handful in-progress (so many character ideas!), all with varying Tav builds and story decisions. There is just so much to do and discover, and so many ways to do it. To fully enjoy this game, you have to dive in; you have to let its world envelop you.

Some games resonate with you in such a way that you'll have no choice but to return to them after a while away. BG3 gives you back ten times as much as you put in, and it will be repeatedly revisited by me for many years to come.

review:
As a casual gamer I am very picky about the games I purchase. I do not like to throw money away needlessly and waited quite some time for a sale before grabbing BG3. Glad I did, but it's a lot to learn.
I played table top D&D when Gygax first created it, but aside from Dragons of Krynn, Pool of Radiance, and a few other early (1995-1999) D&D-based titles haven't touched it since the late 1990's. Setting up options/keystrokes took a few hours going back and forth between changes, short play, and more changes until I had things how I like them. Probably not an issue for a regular Larian or D&D player though.

D&D-style play isn't for everyone, but the game mechanics are handled well and are smooth. I had a rough go for the first 10 hours or so, having to learn and relearn spells, effects, choice outcomes, and generally understanding what causes what. Note that I'm still getting surprises after over 70 hours but they are becoming less frequent. I save frequently, replaying scenarios as I go...sometimes because I made a bad choice; sometimes just to see what else could go on. 

My gripes come from two places:
Learning curve if you don't have a current familiarity with D&D, spell actions, consequences, etc. then play will be frustrating? until you get up to speed.
 
I haven't found an 'UNDO' for a bad (wrong) keystroke other than backing out of a spell with ESC to choose a different action. It's pretty easy to accidentally trigger a wrong keypress on my keyboard and the only correction is to reload. MY bad but it would be nice to have an out.

I'm still in Act 1 and will stay there until I hit at least level 6 (level 7 if I can) before crossing into Act 2. I'm also trying diligently to avoid spoilers and guides although I do have to admit to a few. Buttons are easy to spot in scenes, levers not so much. You'll need to be able to see well, both from your character and your monitor. Managing the camera is an art form.

I'm playing with a C6 tandem 48" OLED, Z690 ASUS Tuf Gaming board, 34GB G.Skill DDR4, MSI RTX 5070 Gaming Trio (12GB VRAM), 14th gen i9 (post 2025 so no burn-up issue) with a Lian Li 360 AIO. All settings on max or ultra. Temps stay between 62 and 71 c for cpu and gpu.

review: I was recommended this by an acquaintance about a month or so after the game released in 2023. I had no context for what the game was, nor had I ever played Dungeons and Dragons at the time. I went in almost entirely blind and I ended up being absolutely blown away. My first playthrough took about 100 hours and then I went and convinced some of my friends to get the game and we did a multiplayer co-op playthrough which took even longer. There is an absolutely insane amount of content here, especially when you consider that your choices can radically alter the events of the game, providing a ton of replay value. The game gives you almost complete freedom to approach any encounter or event in the game however you wish. In the modern day where a lot of games tend to hold the hands of the players to guide them, this game does the opposite most of the time, and that is incredibly refreshing. It doesn't insult your intelligence and gives you the freedom to approach things how you want. The gameplay is very fun and mechanically deep. The story is fantastic and all of the characters are very well written. The world itself is very fascinating. This is easily one of the best RPG games I have ever played, and probably one of the best RPGs ever made.

review:
[h1]Good, just not for me.[/h1]

This will be a negative review but in all fairness the game does deserve a thumbs up.

I tried twice to get into this game in a span of two years. Both times I ended up feeling unattracted to the story. Only the second time was I able to put my finger on exactly what it was.

First, it's the whole D&D thing. I'll start by saying that D&D is not by any stretch a bad game. But if you haven't played it, you WILL find it overwhelming. It requires a lot of time and patience to get to grips with all the mechanics. My problem is that BG3 doesn't do a very good job at delivering it to you piecemeal. From level 1 you are thrown knee-deep into the mechanics of D&D with no safety rails. The result? Combat feels unbalanced in favor of the AI. I think for those of us who have never played D&D, but who wanted to get into the game nonetheless, a beginner-friendly version of each class could've been added, with reduced spells and abilities or a simplified set of rules, just enough to get to grips with the core, and then be given full access to everything later on.

Secondly, it's the characters. They really do feel like caricatures of RPG tropes. Like they have distilled the essence of each stereotypical RPG character, injected it with hormones and steroids, and moulded them into characters that end up feeling unlikeable, tiresome and unidimensional. I just wanted them to shut the hell up and let me play, because I already knew what they would say or how they would act. They are predictable. Furthermore, each one comes packed with their own problem. This would've been cool and interesting were it not for the fact that their problems seem to compete with the main quest in urgency and importance. I stopped playing when I no longer could tell whether the game wanted me to get rid of the worm, or the vampire, or the magic eater, or the guy who explodes. I ended up thinking, damn, give me a break. You have crafted a wonderful world and I cannot slow down and soak it in because you've loaded me with urgent missions from the very start.

Thirdly, the sex. It was not a driving point for me, but still I felt the game pushed it a little too much. While it is avoidable for the most part, there are moments in which I wasn't even sure if a dialogue option would lead to sex. I wish there was an option to just disable all romance mechanics in the game, not just the nudity, but rather turn off all dialogue options to romance characters.

Fourth, I don't think I got hooked onto the world. It all feels too disparate and loose. Again, there are too many things thrown at you from the start, like you're in the middle of a conflict of cosmic proportions, but this depth is lost on a person who has no background knowledge of anything. I failed to be enthralled by it because I didn't get the chance to discover it bit by bit. The opening cinematic shows you so many places, people, creatures, races, etc, that it is just not possible to care for any one of them in particular. 

I played BG1 and while some of the irks I mentioned are also present there (for example the amount of spells and abilities), the story felt a lot more grounded in scale and scope, at least in the beginning, so that by being able to focus on one thing at a time, I felt it to be more compelling and captivating. If BG1 is a nice steak with a side of mash potatoes and a beer, BG3 is an all-you-can-eat buffet with way too many dishes from countries you haven't even heard of, none of them particularly appetizing.

Why have I given it a thumbs up, then? Because in my opinion the game undoubtedly deserves it if you are into D&D, Baldur's Gate or cRPGs in general. I feel like the problems I have listed above mainly come from my not being the target audience of this game, and thus I don't think it fair to negatively affect its score. I really wish I could've been captivated by this game, because it does look like an awesome experience, but alas! It is just not to my taste or expectations, at all.

review:
Baulders Gate 3 is not your ideal fantacy world where everything is perfect; there is constant suffering, struggle and death by both the main, secondary and background characters. You will experience great highs and satisfactory moments, but you will also experience great losses. Losing a character is felt by everyone, including you. There may not always be a way to save someone from dying depending on your choices earlier in the game. There are multiple player choices that will leave a bitter taste due to none of the outcomes being perfect. 

There is so much content and replayability. My first playthrough I got around 60% of the way through in 40 hours or so, my second playthrough took me 45 hours from start to finish. None of the game felt like filler, and everytime I had to reload I was not worried about losing progress due to the massive variety of dialogue options and ways to traverse/clear an area of enemies. Reloading does take a while though, even on a top-end m.2 SSD.

My first and second playthrough were completely different experiences, even though it was the same class build and moral decisions.

Once you get into hubs/towns there is a mindblowing amount of quality content for players. Quests, NPCs, Shop items, Points of Interest, political struggles/strife, etc

Each named NPC has voicelines although not every NPC you can actually talk to; they will say a voice line when you try to talk to them but you cannot reply. Almost all alive and dead NPCs have unique names, aside from unidentifiable skeletons/corpses. Dead NPCs in varying states of decay also have names, and you can talk to some of them some skills/spells.

Had to mod the game to get it in a playable state due to my competitive FPS brain not liking the movement movement and punishing rng mechanics. But aside from those 2 issues, this game is crazy good. I'll probably replay this many times in the future.

This is what a game should look like. Especially if you're a Dragon Age: Origins fan. The encounters and conversations are superb. Gameplay is AMAZING for a strategist. You can do a lot in this game, and it's creative, wondrous, and interactive. 
- Every character and the way they interact is REALISTIC. No of to the sunset hero! kinda dialogue. No simple, cheesy repetitive talk. Just a breeze of good writing that makes you want to learn more. 
- You can plan your game to take different approach towards your enemies. You can set them on fire, or befriend them if you know how. You can turn them into sheep or raise them from the dead! To talk or to fight. You can curse them and many MANY more options.
- A lot of races to choose from -Drow, Dark Elf, Halfelf, demon, dragonborn, etc., and you can somewhat shift their backgrounds and personalities. Other characters will react to this. 
- There is a game difficulty for those gamers who don't get to enjoy challenge that much, Honor Mode. You die once, the adventure is over. you try to turn off the app? it will auto save everything. you will have low stats, while the enemy has realistic amounts of stat buff (It is designed in a particular way so the fight  isn't repetitive in anyway like games who give too much hp to a boss fight or something.) 
- Personaly I think it's a nice touch that you have a Narrator with you when you interact with anything. The voice actress and the team behind it did pretty solid job on this. Feels mystical, adventurous, and unique. 
- The good thing about a game with good story writing is that you might get curious again to see what if you had reacted differently towards something or maybe you want to play the game in a different style.

review:
My first ASW game was BlazBlue Calamity Trigger on the 360 from Blockbuster; ever since getting into BB, I've been trying to get into GG as well, and I just never could click with the series... until now. Strive was absolute shit on launch and put me off the series for a few more years, more so than even XX AC+R's old netcode and Xrd's horrendously hostile playerbase did, but coming back to it recently and with help from a more GG-first friend, I can finally say I absolutely love this game, and coming to enjoy it has been a breath of fresh air.

I know this game has alienated a lot of the hardcore GG fanbase, but honestly, I think this is the game GG needed and, frankly, deserved; the game is much easier to engage with, learn, and get a feel for, but there's still plenty of depth to explore, just without some of the flailing older GG's felt like they encouraged (and no more fucking Danger Time dumpster, hurray!)

With way better lifetime support, content updates, and improvements than any game before it, and with a much broader reach to new players thanks to this game being the first GG to actually have decent marketing, I can highly recommend this as a stepping-on point for anyone still wondering if getting into GG in the big '26 and beyond is worthwhile. Hell, thanks to this game, I've even gone back and started enjoying the other GG games I mentioned earlier! review:
After spending over 100 hours and finally reaching Vanquisher, my opinion of this game remains the same as it was when it first released, in that it's a step down in almost every way when compared to the game that came before it. I recognize that doesn't mean much considering that a lot of other people who have spent way more time on this game still recommend it, and i don't think that me reaching Vanquisher is indicative of my skills or knowledge as a player. But nevertheless, i dedicated a considerable amount of time into this game and have amassed a lot of knowledge about the game mechanics, so i think my opinion should still count for something, even if it's not a lot.

For starters i would like to address the amount of content present in the base game, which is what i stuck with, i didn't buy any of the DLC characters. I'm not going to complain about the roster size or the fact that you can't unlock DLC characters with the in game money you get from winning fights like in XRD SIGN, that's just par for the course these days, but what i am going to complain about is the lack of fun and unique single player modes like M.O.M or even just combo trials (my favorite mode), which are present, but the quality varies due to the fact they're community made. I understand that this game had some issues with development because of Covid, but i don't see any reason why they couldn't add these features in an update, despite the fact that this game has been out for about 5 years. And who in the world actually cares about Team of 3 mode?

But the main reason why i cannot recommend this game is because of how it tries to make things more accessible, that is by lowering the skill floor, while at the same time lowering the skill ceiling. The restricted gatling system, the reworked character movesets that removed a lot of their tools, and the absence of instant kills still bothers me to this day. Some of the new mechanics that are added in this game are interesting and provide more options for player expression I'll admit, like the movement options after Roman Canceling, but they don't serve as a replacement for all the things that were removed. Despite the fact that i had an easier time learning this game due to the things that were simplified, i still prefer games like XRDRev2 or BBCF, because even though I'm getting mauled by every player i manage to come across online, it's so much more interesting to learn those games than it is with Strive. I get that, my opinion doesn't apply to everyone, and hey judging by how well this game sold compared to those games, it's obvious that simplifying the game was at least successful at attracting new players. But going forward i hope the devs at ArcSys aren't afraid to make games that are more in depth an complex, because i even if i get beaten up and lose all the time, i don't mind that as long as the game is interesting. But to me, Guilty Gear Strive is just not very interesting. I feel like I've experienced all that i can with this game, and now I'm left feeling dissatisfied, wanting more. But who knows, maybe something about it will change in the future that pulls me back in, i really hope so. I wouldn't have written down all of this if i didn't like guilty gear, because i really do, and one day i hope i can like it again with all my heart.

review:
Really fun, but I hate fighting games. I really appreciate this game because it was a fighting game I could get into it. The amazing visuals & animation definitely pulled me in. The characters all have distinct personalities & great designs. The music is good too. 

Overall, I though the combat was great. The amazing art made it feel really good & look very cool. It is definitely accessible to get into, and I recommend it if you don't have experience with the genre (like me). Landing hits & winning just feels super satisfying in this game. 

However, I think fighting games still aren't for me. I'm just not the biggest fan of memorizing random inputs & hoping my directional inputs are even correct. These games just feel kind of restrictive to me, and I prefer being able to improvise with different tools. In addition, I think some characters just have super annoying combos. I've played a lot of games where I still had fun losing, but I just give up when somebody uses a character with some insane combo and I can't do anything. Also, I think too much of the roster is paid DLC. 

Still, I'm glad I gave this game a try & I did enjoy it a bit, but I got burnt out of it so quickly. I just don't think grinding to get good is gonna feel worth it or fun at all to me. I'll come to this game eventually.
